newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: ELECTION FRENZY GRIPS EX-SOVIET MOLDOVA.
newsitem.headline: ELECTION FRENZY GRIPS EX-SOVIET MOLDOVA.

text.p: The three leading candidates in Molodova's first multi-party presidential election wound up a frenzied campaign on Friday by underlining differences they say will determine the former Soviet republic's fate.

But with the local media support divided, posters of all three plastered over the capital and no reliable opinion polls, it is hard to predict whether the current president, the prime minister or the chairman of parliament will come out on top.

Apart from varying personal styles, the three men, who are leading a pack of nine candidates for Sunday's election, have differing attitudes to the key issues of the campaign -- relations with Russia and neighbouring Romania.
Mircea Snegur, president since 1991, has conducted an aggressive, populist campaign, underlining his cool attitude to Russia and his pro-Romanian leanings.

Quietly-spoken prime minister Andrei Sangheli is trying to persuade voters that the future of Moldova's struggling economy is inextricably linked with Russia and not Romania, while Petru Lucinschi, parliament chairman, treads somewhere in between.

Russia's communist-dominated parliament fuelled the fire by voting on Wednesday in favour of closer ties with Moldova's breakaway Dnestr region, most of whose 700,000 people are Slavs, unlike the majority population in the republic who share a language and culture with Romania.
The move has infuriated Chisinau and may play into the hands of nationalists like Snegur who favour closer ties between Romania and Moldova.
The 56-year-old president built on his image as a man of the people on Friday with a trip to his native village of Trifanesti to get a public blessing from his mother.

The president's powers are limited in Moldova and Snegur has pledged, if he wins, to get rid of the "corrupt" government and parliament headed by his two main rivals in the race and set up a presidential state.

Sangheli, who like other contenders has been chasing rural vote in the mostly agricultural state of 4.3 million, on Friday addressed thousands of workers at a flour mill -- a considerable boost for a candidate widely seen as uncharismatic.

Without naming Snegur, Sangheli attacked "those people who led us towards a catastrophe under the drumbeating of patriotic slogans", clearly referring to a 1992 bloody conflict with the Dnestr separatists in which hundreds were killed.
While Snegur has been unable to reach a political settlement with the Dnestr leaders, Sangheli has been working hard to restore some ties with Moldova's industrial heartland.
Speaker after speaker at the rally praised Sangheli, 52, as a man of few words and many deeds and "the only man who enjoys trust of both Moscow and Tiraspol (the Dnestr capital)".

"We are in favour of closer integration with the Commonwealth of Independent States...This is our market and we get our fuel and energy from it," he told Reuters, referring to Romania as only "a neighbour with whom we should live normally".
Lucinschi, 56, a charismatic intellectual who presents himself as an independent centrist, took a cautious line.
"I do not depend on any party or business group and so there is a chance to create a new atmosphere in society," he said in an hour-long radio phone-in programme.
Most analysts agree that none of the candidates will win a 50 percent majority on Sunday and predict a runoff round between the two top contenders on December 1.

The Dnestr authorities have banned the poll on their territory but local residents may travel to vote outside Dnestr. High turnout there and across the country, landlocked between Romania and Ukraine, is expected to favour Sangheli.
